Modified assessment incorporating Beige Book evidence:
- Economic activity: Beige Book references point to broad March–April weakness across districts, with consumer spending sharply lower—especially for auto dealers and general retailers—reinforcing the FOMC’s description of “sharp declines in economic activity.” (Consumer Spending impacts Auto Dealers/General Retailers; Economic Activity occurs in March/April; reports on districts.)
- Manufacturing: Activity weakened amid uncertainty, consistent with trade-related headwinds noted in the Beige Book references and now compounded by COVID-19. (Manufacturing activity affected by trade-related uncertainty; reports on districts.)
- Employment: Beige Book notes sectoral stress, including tourism, aligning with widespread job losses. Any earlier skilled-labor shortages are overshadowed by layoffs and hiring freezes. (Tourism reports on districts; labor markets cited shortages of skilled laborers.)
- Prices/inflation: Overall inflation pressures remain muted, with input costs mixed—freight, metals, tariffs, wages, and natural gas influencing prices—but weak demand and lower oil keep headline pressures subdued. (Prices influenced by freight costs, metal prices, tariffs, wages, natural gas.)
- Agriculture: Crop price pressures vary by commodity, and weather effects (flooding/rainfall) add localized strain, contributing to uneven rural conditions. (Crop price pressures vary by commodity; agricultural conditions impacted by flooding/rainfall.)
- Credit channel overlay (SLOOS): Banks tightened standards and widened spreads across C&I/CRE and selected consumer products, and demand weakened—particularly in CRE—indicating bank-intermediated credit will amplify the downturn despite Fed backstops.

Implication: The Beige Book corroborates and slightly deepens the downside risks flagged by the FOMC and SLOOS—broad-based activity declines, severe sectoral hits (tourism, autos, retail), muted inflation, and tighter credit—so the sentiment is revised modestly more negative.
